https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/lov.s: Loving your neighbor as yourself targets the root of sin, pride, by redirecting natural self-love toward God so it overflows in generous love.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/son.s: Jesus shows that Psalm 110 points to a Messiah who is both David’s descendant and his divine Lord, who died, rose and reigns at God’s right hand as priest-king.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Jesus’ blessings are both present and still future, so God’s mercy works in believers now, enabling them to become the people He describes.

https://coe22.com/sermons/matthew-mounta.s: Asks whether you are pursuing happiness or the kind of blessing that can’t be shaken.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/ble.s: Jesus blesses not the self-sufficient but those who honestly recognize their helplessness and sin and turn to God’s grace.
Meekness isn’t frailty but God-anchored confidence: handing over burdens, staying calm in waiting, resisting fretful anger and remaining teachable.
Mercy grows from a heart humbled by undeserved grace, and merciful people, balancing mercy with justice, will receive mercy.
Jesus cares most about the inner heart, and purity means wholehearted devotion to God alone, the prerequisite for seeing Him.
God’s children reflect their peace-loving Father by praying for and reaching out to others, while holding to truth and putting righteousness above mere quiet.
Righteous living provokes opposition because it exposes sin, but Jesus promises a greater heavenly reward, so believers can rejoice in suffering.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/t.s: Jesus protects our happiness from both hardship and success by anchoring it in the eternal reward of heaven.

https://coe22.com/sermons/matthew-mounta.s: Matthew 5:13–20: people notice our faith most when we meet hardship with a calm that doesn’t make sense, and it urges believers to live as salt and light.

https://coe22.com/sermons/best-sermon-ev.s: We are not saved by our good works but by Christ’s finished work, yet we are saved for good works.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Fear and guilt don’t reshape us deeply; finding joy in God softens hearts and drives wholehearted obedience.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/get.s: Before bringing offerings to God, pursue reconciliation with those we’ve wronged, since mending relationships matters more than giving.

https://coe22.com/sermons/best-sermon-ev.s: A holy God reconciled sinners through His Son’s blood, and the reconciled are sent as ambassadors of that reconciliation, because forgiven people forgive.
Marriage as a lifelong, God-ordained covenant between one man and one woman, not a mere contract.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/a-p.s: Resisting sexual temptation means actively replacing lustful images with vivid pictures of the crucified Christ, rather than merely praying and hoping it fades.

https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/i.s: Whether backing out of a commitment is sinful depends on how qualified it was, whether changing plans would be more loving, and whether you can honestly ask to be released.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/woe.s: Christians will face opposition, so Jesus calls them to love enemies through discerning, sometimes costly acts, rooted in the grace shown to them as enemies.

https://coe22.com/sermons/best-sermon-ev.s: We are to love our enemies because while we were God’s enemies, He loved us first.

https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/w.s: Jesus’ call to love enemies reaches past persecutors to irritating relatives, unhelpful spouses and indifferent passersby.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jes.s: Jesus is engaged to His people, died to win them and promises to return for the wedding, so believers should stay spiritually alert rather than merely outwardly religious.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/bet.s: Harsh views of God reveal more about our hearts than His character; He is kinder than we imagine, as the parable of the talents shows.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/hav.s: God entrusts everyone with valuable gifts to use faithfully, a reality that both humbles us and frees us from comparing ourselves with others.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/doi.s: Genuine believers feel drawn to relieve others’ suffering, prioritizing fellow Christians while also reaching unbelievers in hope they will know Christ.

https://coe22.com/sermons/matthew-old-to.s: Matthew 11: John the Baptist’s doubt in prison shows that doubt doesn’t disqualify faith, and the real battle is faith versus fear.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/meeting-.s: Keller says people offended by Jesus’ claims about himself are spiritually closed, and names three kinds of people open to meeting him: the poor, the violent and the least.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/rejectin.s: Keller explores why many reject Jesus, describing unbelief as a failure of wisdom, of not seeing what is truly real, and looks at the power and character of unbelief and its remedy.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-grea.s: Jesus answers doubts like John the Baptist’s with a striking claim about his own greatness. Keller says it should jolt listeners out of complacency and into childlike humility.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/will-he.s: Jesus indicates certain towns will face harsher judgment than Sodom, since they witnessed His miracles yet refused to repent.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/miracle.s: Miracles are meant to lead people to turn from sin toward God, and treating them merely as blessings misses their aim.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-grac.s: Keller looks at Jesus’ claim that he alone makes the Father known, arguing it rests on a deeper claim about who Jesus is, and asks why it is credible and how to live in light of it.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/god-mus.s: Only God can open our eyes to know Him; human wisdom, strength and wealth cannot lead anyone to Him without His self-revelation.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-grea.s: Keller argues Jesus offers deep inner rest for the soul, not just physical rest, and covers why people need it, what it is and how to receive it.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/is-his-.s: Asks whether Jesus’ burden truly feels light, stressing that eternal life comes through Christ alone while many paths lead to ruin.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/we-cann.s: Spiritual sight of Jesus is impossible apart from God’s revealing, since many who saw or read about Him never recognized or worshiped Him.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/god-hid.s: God’s saving truth is concealed from the self-assured and revealed to the humble (Matthew 11:25–30).

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/how.s: Real discipleship puts Jesus above every other desire, accepts hardship for His sake and follows wholeheartedly rather than only when comfortable.

https://coe22.com/sermons/matthew-fear-t.s: Poses the question of whether you need a miracle.
Storms are inevitable, but fear doesn’t have to be.

https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/w.s: Jesus frees the demon-possessed men and restores their humanity, while the lost pigs test whether people choose Jesus over material wealth.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/s.s: Because Satan’s defeat is certain and he knows it, believers can mock his temptations, and the church works as a dangerous covert resistance against his realm.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/what-gr.s: People aren’t lost from a shortage of God’s compassion but because stubborn, defiant hearts don’t delight in the compassionate God.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-lord.s: Keller says Jesus came not to improve religious practice but to end it by offering himself in its place, contrasting the emptiness of earning God’s favor with the completeness found in Christ.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-fina.s: Jesus’ claim to be the final word, with salvation entirely by grace, so offended the Pharisees and Herodians that they plotted his death. Keller adds that the real Jesus draws and repels people at once, exposing divisions in our own hearts.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/a-new-sa.s: Keller looks at two Sabbath incidents, Jesus’ anger, his opponents and the huge claim he makes about himself, and argues that claim reshapes how believers understand the Sabbath.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/with-jes.s: After gaining popularity, Jesus goes up a mountain to name his disciples. Keller says this shows how Jesus transforms people, and covers how and why that happens.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Rejecting the Holy Spirit can leave a person unable to repent, which makes that particular sin unforgivable (Mark 3:20–35).

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/bey.s: Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit so hardens a person that they can no longer repent, and listeners are urged to repent now.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-fami.s: Keller argues Jesus must be understood as he presents himself in Mark, not as a figure shaped by our wishes. He weighs mistaken views of Jesus, Jesus’ own claims and how they should shape our lives.

https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/h.s: Scripture honors Mary as blessed, but Jesus redirects admiration to those who obey God’s word, so imitate her faith rather than elevate her as a mediator.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/jesus-an.s: Using Pilate’s questions to Jesus and the crowd, Keller explores how Christianity relates to government and offers three answers: ambiguity, revolution and substitution.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/mocking-.s: Keller looks at how Jesus is mocked, insulted and shamed at the start of the crucifixion, arguing the mockery exposes our own hearts, reveals Jesus’ heart and can reshape ours.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Demanding signs can mask a heart craving human approval more than God, blinding people to the self-giving love Christ displayed on the cross.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-deat.s: Keller treats the supernatural darkness at Jesus’ death as a sign: the darkness humanity faces, the darkness Jesus absorbed in its place, and how his suffering can lift ours.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/hav.s: Even when suffering feels like abandonment, God is working through the pain to deepen faith and bring lasting good.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/women-pa.s: Jesus’ burial brings together a Roman centurion, the women who stayed, and Joseph of Arimathea, a Pharisee. Keller uses them to ask what kind of world people long for, what change is needed and how it can happen.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/with-a-r.s: Keller says Jesus challenged ritual washings to show that everyone feels spiritually unclean and tries to cleanse themselves in their own ways, which never work, and points to what does.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-symp.s: The only recorded time Jesus left Israel’s borders is no accident, Keller says, and the healings of a Gentile girl and a deaf-mute man are meant to teach something about his compassion and character.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/god.s: Marriage and children both draw their meaning from God: marriage pictures Christ’s covenant love for the church, children show the dependence needed to enter the kingdom.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/wha.s: Marriage portrays Christ’s faithful, never-ending commitment to His church, so Jesus calls us to lifelong vows while offering forgiveness to those who have failed.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/become-a.s: Keller explains the cross two ways: Jesus settled the debt that separates people from God, and that grace frees believers to approach God with the confidence of children.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the.s: Opposing abortion isn’t enough; true pro-life living overcomes self-centered indifference to inconvenient people, from children to the elderly, and reflects Christ’s welcoming compassion.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/mis.s: Because salvation depends on God’s power and Christ repays every sacrifice many times over, believers should pursue overseas missions as a path to deeper joy.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/camels-a.s: Keller says the “camel and needle” saying is about the basics of salvation, not just ethics: why wealth is a spiritual danger to becoming a Christian and how believers can handle that risk.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/m.s: Missionaries gain encouragement and modesty by recognizing that God’s sovereign grace supplies all their strength and fruit, guarding against despair and arrogance.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/r.s: Whatever believers surrender for Christ, He repays far more abundantly, so any sacrifice ends as gain rather than loss.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/gre.s: Humility means relying on God and giving Him credit for everything; rooted in the gospel it moves us to serve and produces joy, courage and diligence.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-mean.s: Keller argues Jesus came primarily to die, unlike founders of other religions who came to teach a way of life, and explains why the cross was necessary and how it should transform believers.

https://coe22.com/sermons/when-he-asks/w.s: Closes a seven-week series by asking whether we still feel real awe about Jesus, and invites fresh eyes on Him through Mark 10:32–52.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: True worship treasures Christ above everything, so genuine Christians are marked by joyful, heart-level satisfaction in God rather than mere religious activity.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/cross-th.s: Keller says the cross reshapes how Christians see the world and moves them toward service and mission, presenting Jesus’ self-sacrifice as a redeeming payment that gives believers a fresh direction.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/was-jes.s: People admire Jesus as an ethical sage like Socrates, but the biblical portrait rules out treating Him as merely a teacher.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Explores how Jesus serves those who worship Him, drawing on Mark 10:45.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/arguing-.s: Keller looks at how religious leaders tried to trap Jesus into taking a political side, and argues his answer about taxes reshapes the debate beyond ordinary politics.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/obey-as.s: Believers freed by Christ willingly submit to human authorities, and that humble, law-abiding witness shows the world the true nature of Christian liberty.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/arguing-.s: Keller asks what it means to live a moral life, covering the problem everyone faces, the kind of life people need and the journey required to get there.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/sma.s: Christ treasures tiny communities, understands the hardships of pastors serving there, and plans to bring people to salvation through their faithful labor.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-man-.s: Jesus is offensive to every culture, Keller says, because the gospel declares human achievements worthless and salvation dependent on Jesus alone. In the Gospels people either opposed Jesus or worshipped him and gave up everything to follow.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/watching.s: Keller reads Jesus’ warning that Jerusalem’s coming destruction foreshadows the end of the world and his return, and takes up doubts about it: whether it breeds fanaticism, what difference it makes and what watchfulness looks like.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/man-in-t.s: Jesus is presented as the anointed King and Son of God, not merely a great leader or an angel. Keller’s three points: who the King is, how people meet him in the wilderness, and where he is heading, the cross.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/riv.s: John’s wilderness baptism across the Jordan signals a fresh exodus and renewed covenant, preparing God’s people to follow a new Joshua into a new kingdom.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/mar.s: John the Baptist’s testimony about Jesus’ might, saving work and worth invites us to make Christ, not the holiday, our greatest delight.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/father-s.s: Keller presents the Trinity as one God in three persons who love each other, and argues that Jesus’ baptism shows our deepest need is to be drawn into that relationship.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/called-t.s: Keller argues Jesus’ call to follow him is distinct, demanding, growth-oriented and achievable, and that a Jesus shaped to fit our preferences cannot challenge or change us.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Demonic forces are subject to Jesus’ authority (Mark 1:27), so Satan has no independent power beyond the Lord’s control.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/called-t.s: Keller argues that knowing who Jesus is comes before grasping his mission, and presents him as a king over salvation, the mind, the heart and the direction of one’s life, who can be trusted.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/no-.s: Ordinary daily tasks gain lasting significance when done in grateful response to Jesus’ kindness, as Simon’s mother-in-law’s serving after her healing shows.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/a-leper-.s: Jesus’ healing of the leper shows what his kingdom is like, restoring the man physically, emotionally, socially and religiously, and points ahead to the renewal of all creation through his authoritative word.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-heal.s: Keller looks at Jesus healing a paralyzed man and forgiving his sins, showing Jesus’ authority and provoking the leaders’ anger, and argues the passage challenges, comforts and empowers the reader.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/a-paraly.s: Keller retells the paralytic lowered through a roof and how Jesus’ actions shock three groups: the man seeking healing, readers of the story and the religious leaders.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/who.s: In a screen-saturated age, Christ alone must capture our hearts, since drifting affections lead us to seek satisfaction in digital distractions.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/fai.s: From the father’s plea in Mark 9: Jesus rebukes hesitant, conditional prayer, since faith trusts God’s power and goodness and unbelief is the real barrier.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/rec.s: Christ redirects the drive to be significant toward humble service, and welcoming children in Jesus’ name means welcoming God.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/he-.s: Jesus welcomed a woman’s costly perfume offering, seeing love where critics saw waste; lavish devotion to Christ is never wasted.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-betr.s: Jesus predicts one disciple will betray him and all will abandon him. Keller uses this to teach the breadth and depth of sin and how to overcome it, especially for people who think they are close to Jesus.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/joi.s: Christianity is inherently a singing faith because God is infinitely joyful, and His children sing to release their own delight in Him.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/witness-.s: Keller sets Peter’s denial beside Jesus’ arrest and trial, treating Peter as a defendant too. No one naturally has the integrity to speak the truth about Jesus at any cost, but Peter’s failure was followed by restoration and faithful witness.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-hear.s: Keller looks at Jesus’ anguish in Gethsemane, facing death in distress rather than composure, and what it reveals about the reality of the cross, God’s wrath and how believers can face suffering.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-fide.s: In Gethsemane, as the disciples sleep and Jesus faces death, Keller argues lasting change comes from a heart transformed by focusing on Jesus, not from obeying rules out of fear or self-interest.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the.s: Jesus’ willing agony in Gethsemane, choosing His Father’s will before Calvary, reveals a unique sacrificial love to marvel at rather than merely imitate.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-kiss.s: Keller treats Jesus’ arrest as a clash between worldly values and those of his kingdom, and through Judas, Peter and the unnamed young man examines how hard it is to live in that kingdom and where the power comes from.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/christs-.s: Keller shows Jesus on trial as both the judge and the one who is judged, and argues that holding both truths together should change how we live.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/whe.s: Earliest Greek manuscripts and the harder reading suggest Mark originally ended at 16:8, though the longer ending remains useful.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-empt.s: Keller argues Mark’s brief empty-tomb account holds the whole message of Easter: a call to change your mind, receive grace that changes your heart, and take up a mission that reshapes your life.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: From Mark 4:1–20: the enemy works to steal God’s message from people before it can take root and grow.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-seed.s: Using the parable of the seed, Keller argues the gospel has real power to change lives, releases it in its own way, and that its apparent weakness is the source of its strength.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/sat.s: The devil snatches God’s message from listeners through distraction, hostility, persecution and materialism, threatening fruitfulness and discipleship.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/fai.s: Success in mission work comes from steadily spreading the gospel, not counting visible results, because God alone controls the harvest.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/s.s: Hardship can shatter belief rather than strengthen it, but trusting that God delivers grace through pain helps faith endure and grow.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-open.s: Keller explains why the kingdom of God matters, the principle that organizes it, and how believers receive the power to live by that principle, calling the kingdom central to Jesus’ message in Mark.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-powe.s: Keller argues Jesus’ gentle care and his sovereign power over storms belong together, drawing four lessons: Christ’s power is real, vast, divine and compatible with life’s hardships.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/lord-of-.s: Jesus is shown as a real Savior rather than a projected one, Keller says, whose power is real-world, infinite, unmanageable and costly, from the King’s Cross series on Mark.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-defe.s: On the longest exorcism account in the Bible, Keller examines the complexity of evil, how it takes hold in a life and how it can be defeated.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/with-a-t.s: Keller argues Jesus took demon possession seriously as a real condition, not ignorance, and draws three lessons on how evil operates, how it recurs and how healing happens.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/tel.s: Reaching the lost is the church’s unfinished mission from Christ, a top priority that flows from and fuels love for God’s glory.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-timi.s: Keller looks at how Jesus’ delays test our patience, what those delays teach, and the puzzling weakness Jesus shows in the account.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-fina.s: Keller reads the triumphal entry, the temple cleansing and the fig tree together to show Jesus’ character and power, and how that power shapes the character of his followers.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/he-.s: Jesus’ cursing of the fruitless fig tree symbolized Israel’s spiritual emptiness, and by bearing a curse on the cross He turned death into life for all nations.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/una.s: Delayed answers to prayer should lead us to examine our trust and deepen our relationship with God rather than give up praying.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/s.s: Christ provides for those who serve: the leftovers from the feedings were for the servers, so no one outgives Jesus.

https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/w.s: God’s comprehensive control is inseparable from the gospel, since He purposefully wove together Christ’s suffering, rejection and death, and seeing this moves us to worship.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Jesus’ death was planned by the Father and willingly embraced by the Son to ransom many, and following Him means valuing Him above comfort and reputation.

https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/m.s: Jesus is worth more than wealth and human approval; clinging to possessions or admiration leads to spiritual loss, while losing them for Christ brings life.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/den.s: Self-denial doesn’t make Christians miserable; it leads to our true selves, resistance against the devil, alignment with God and freedom from sorrow.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/being-a.s: Being ashamed to publicly identify with Jesus exposes a person’s true standing, and heaven belongs to those who openly embrace Him in this life.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/to-.s: Nothing the world offers is worth trading your soul for, so value eternal well-being above comfort, bodily concerns and material gain.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: On Luke 17:1–10: treat sin as seriously as Jesus does, and ask how far love should go to protect others from it.
Jesus’ mustard seed comparison shows even tiny faith is effective because its power comes from God, not from the believer’s size.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/generosi.s: Keller says real generosity includes releasing people who have wronged you, not just giving money, and presents forgiveness as the central form of relational generosity.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/how.s: Faith grows not by measuring how much we have but by trusting God’s power and knowing His grace reaches us whether we succeed or still fall short.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the.s: Piper praises God for answered prayer on a busy Sunday and urges the church to pray as major expansion decisions loom.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/jes.s: From the ten lepers: ingratitude is a sin that stings, yet Jesus presses on in joy and love rather than dwelling on the hurt.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/forgiven.s: Discipleship means habitual, ongoing forgiveness, Keller says, and he asks why we need a forgiving spirit, what it is and how to get it.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/is-.s: God’s kingdom has already broken into history through Christ, but its full realization waits for His second coming, so believers live between now and then.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/w.s: Watching a vivid thunderstorm from a plane led Piper to reflect on Christ’s dazzling return and to invite delighting in God through joy in Him.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/joh.s: True repentance means abandoning trust in ancestry or good works and relying on God’s undeserved mercy, since judgment applies regardless of heritage.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/preparin.s: Keller draws on John the Baptist’s preparation of people to show how we receive Jesus as King: by relying on him, obeying him, relaxing in his rule and expecting him to act.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/wha.s: Real repentance shows in how we handle money: we stop exploiting others and generously share, trusting God’s mercy more than wealth.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: In Luke 3, Jesus’ baptism marks the Spirit’s gentle, dove-like commissioning, and His Adam-linked genealogy highlights His universal humanity.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-cros.s: Keller looks at Jesus clearing the temple, the only violent act of his recorded in Scripture, and what the temple meant and what its cleansing reveals about the cross.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/thi.s: Jesus welcomes society’s outcasts and eats with them to show God’s heart for gathering guests, while self-focused religious people miss the invitation.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/he-welco.s: Keller reads the lost sheep, lost coin and lost son together, arguing God’s grace both transforms individuals and forms believers into a distinctive kind of community.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Jesus eats with sinners because God is glad to welcome every lost person to His table (Luke 15:1–2).

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/mis.s: God calls everyone to share His joy, and the church must urgently reach outsiders with the gospel, since the table is not yet full.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Heaven celebrates when a sinner turns back to God, showing the Lord takes joy in searching out and rescuing the lost (Luke 15:1–10).

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Jesus welcoming sinners shows God actively pursuing the lost, and heaven celebrates each person who repents and returns.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: From the prodigal son: God eagerly embraces returning sinners with joy rather than reluctance.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/he-came-.s: Keller says God’s grace restores broken community through repentance, as the younger son shows in returning to his father, and looks at why repentance matters, what it is and how to practice it.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/com.s: God watches for wandering people, and when they return in genuine repentance He welcomes them with generous, joyful love.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: From Luke 15:11–24: God’s heart is full of joy and eagerness to welcome sinners home, like the father who runs to his returning son.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/and-kiss.s: From the prodigal son, Keller shows how a father’s forgiveness and welcome model what forgiveness looks like: assertive, sacrificial, powered from within and leading to a kind of resurrection.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-true.s: Keller argues that being lost is not only for the openly rebellious but can affect religious insiders like the elder brother, and covers what it is, how to recognize it and how to respond.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/we-had-t.s: Keller connects humanity’s spiritual homesickness to the Bible’s story of exile and homecoming, arguing the parable explains the human condition, God’s solution and the new fellowship that results.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Seeing God as a demanding master whose favor must be earned warps our hearts and breeds resentment toward grace; honor Him by trusting Him as a loving Father.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/a-t.s: Through the prodigal son, Jesus shows the self-righteous older brother that the Father lovingly pleads with him to join the celebration.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Seeing God merely as a strict Lord can hide the delight of belonging to Him as family, leaving us resentful outside the party.
From Luke 15:25–31: God wants us to relate to Him as beloved children rather than dutiful servants who merely perform tasks.
Heaven celebrates when a lost sinner is found, showing God’s deep delight in seeking and restoring those who have wandered.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/faith-in.s: Faith connects people to Jesus’ healing, within us and between us, Keller says, and through the Roman centurion and a woman of the street he argues nobody’s background puts them beyond its reach.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/gods-lo.s: Jesus’ question about who loves more, the much-forgiven or the little-forgiven, deepens our love for Christ (Luke 7:36–50).

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/forgive.s: Faces a hard text where Jesus’ words seem to clash with core beliefs, digging deeper to find harmony with the rest of Scripture.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/with-the.s: Keller contrasts Simon, a religious insider, with a sinful woman who both come to Jesus, and argues that their different understandings of him lead to very different responses from him.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/t.s: Trusting God’s ongoing grace, grounded in Jesus’ forgiveness, frees believers from shame that lingers too long.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/generosi.s: Keller argues generosity of time, talents and gifts grows from discipleship and costly grace and shows up in service to others.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/messenge.s: Every disciple of Jesus is a messenger with a mission, a message and a motivation, Keller says. The message is the gospel, shared publicly with an appeal to believe.

https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/d.s: Believers in a judged city aren’t condemned with it, since God saves individuals; they may suffer historical judgment as purification or be spared through an escape.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/pea.s: Lasting joy rests on God’s completed salvation in Christ rather than ministry results, which otherwise swing us between pride and discouragement.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/you.s: Ministry can lure our hearts toward admiring the good work God does through us over the salvation He has given; Jesus urges gladness that our names are in heaven.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/w.s: Jesus, filled with the Spirit, rejoices because the Father reveals the Son to the humble and hides Him from the self-assured.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/jes.s: Salvation is a supernatural act, planned by the Father and chosen by the Son, so it deserves joyful gratitude rather than casual indifference.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/mer.s: Christians shouldn’t withdraw from political seasons but show neighborly mercy to everyone, checking fears, humbling opinions and listening with curiosity.

https://coe22.com/sermons/the-storytelle.s: God didn’t give you all you have so you could have all you want, but so others could have all they need.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/lov.s: The Good Samaritan redirects us from deciding who deserves love to examining our own compassion, urging practical mercy toward the unborn.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/tow.s: The parable’s call to love neighbors is bound to Luke’s themes of repentance, forgiveness and faith in Christ’s blood, and compassion pushes us toward those in need.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/wha.s: Believers should reject choosing between easing earthly suffering and warning of eternal judgment, since Jesus showed compassion for both.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/whe.s: Busy believers should prioritize time with Jesus as Mary did, so their service flows from a restful relationship with Him.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/prayer/.s: Keller uses Mary at Jesus’ feet to show that disciples are called into a deeply personal relationship with him, and explores what it involves and how to nurture it through prayer.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/awa.s: Martha’s busy serving pulled her attention from Jesus while Mary’s focused devotion left her awake; put Christ before endless activity.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/onl.s: Despite busy lives, our priority is sitting with Jesus and receiving spiritual nourishment from Him, because He alone is essential.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/one.s: Genuine resolutions expose what we truly desire and cost us other pleasures, so audit your time and let every commitment serve your delight in Jesus.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/with-a-p.s: Keller looks at Jesus’ deliberately ambiguous answer to Pilate about his politics, arguing Jesus is not political in the usual sense yet is political in a deeper way.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-king.s: Keller contrasts the many onlookers who fail to grasp what is happening at the crucifixion with the one who recognizes Jesus, and asks which group listeners belong to.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/fat.s: Ignorance remains guilty when truth is available, applied to abortion, where people should recognize what they are doing and seek forgiveness.

https://coe22.com/sermons/tetelestai/tet.s: Liar, lunatic or Lord: those are the only options for deciding who Jesus was and is.
A message on grace at the cross: the man on the middle cross said you could come.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/e.s: Even a late change like the thief’s in his final hours matters greatly, so keep seeking God, who has purposes for the timing.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/tod.s: Both thieves sought rescue, but only the repentant one feared God, admitted guilt, honored Jesus’ innocence and pleaded for mercy, so Christ promised him paradise.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/int.s: Learn from Jesus’ death how to die: trusting that God reigns, pities us and holds our spirits in open hands, even in suffering.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/respondi.s: Keller examines how four groups respond to Jesus at the crucifixion despite widespread rejection, and what that teaches about responding to him in a life-changing way.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/ste.s: When darkness lasts so long that faithfulness feels pointless, keep obeying God, as Joseph of Arimathea did, trusting light will return.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Why Jesus willingly joins sinners at their meals: His purpose is to go after those who are spiritually lost (Luke 19:1–10).
Finding deeper delight in Jesus is what loosens our grip on wealth and frees us from loving earthly possessions most (Luke 19:1–10).

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/generosi.s: Keller says Zacchaeus’ wealth and power matter less than his encounter with Jesus, which transformed his life, and frames the story around the necessity, circumstances, key and sign of conversion.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/with-the.s: Anyone can approach Jesus through the story of Zacchaeus, but money is always a complicating issue for those who come to him.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/pal.s: Jesus’ tears over Jerusalem reveal a mighty mercy that is tenderly moved, self-denying and helpful, and calls believers to imitate it toward those in need.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-robb.s: Keller reads Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem as a call to meet him personally, not just understand him, and presents a king who is real, transforms people, works through paradox and confronts.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/o-t.s: Jesus is always ready to reconcile with whoever embraces the terms of peace He offers, and Luke 19 shows His grief when Jerusalem spurned them.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/he-.s: Jesus wept over Jerusalem during His Palm Sunday entry, grieving her rejection even as crowds hailed Him, yet faced the cross with hope in the joy ahead.

https://coe22.com/sermons/the-storytelle.s: Being rich toward God means using temporary resources to build His eternal kingdom rather than your own short-lived one.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Real wealth comes from belonging to God, not accumulated possessions, so don’t trust riches as your security (Luke 12:13–21).

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/how-mone.s: Keller says Jesus’ conversation with his disciples about money is key to understanding who he is, and follows it from a request to a refusal to a rebuke.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: True wealth isn’t measured by possessions; trusting God endures long after any riches (Luke 12:13–21).

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let.s: Money reveals what our hearts treasure, so Jesus warns against trusting wealth for life; use what you earn to honor God and bless others.
Money isn’t the problem; the danger is wealth pulling our hearts from God, who should be our true treasure.
Wealth isn’t wrong in itself but lures us to seek satisfaction in God’s gifts instead of God; habits like savoring Jesus, trusting His provision and giving resist the pull.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Luke 12:22–31: Jesus leads believers out of anxiety into confident, fearless trust that brings freedom in God’s kingdom.
Remembering God’s eternal promises quiets present fears about the future (Luke 12:22–31).

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/god.s: Worry does nothing to protect life while sensible caution does; Jesus’ command not to be anxious means trusting God, not ignoring safety.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/g.s: Jesus assures believers that God delights to give them His kingdom, so His goodness isn’t reluctant, forced or rooted in anger.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/seek-th.s: Our priorities deeply affect our inner well-being, and riches stored in heaven bring greater contentment than earthly possessions.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/how-mone.s: Anxiety about money runs deep, Keller says, and Jesus addresses it by showing why money holds such power over us and how to break its hold.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/forward-.s: Faith in Jesus doesn’t only bring inner peace but reorders a whole life, Keller argues, as he examines the power, practices and provision of God’s kingdom.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Jesus’ coming stirs division before true peace arrives (Luke 12:49–59).

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/i-came-t.s: Keller explores how Jesus’ self-centered teaching divides people and how his self-denying love caused him constant agony through his ministry.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/work-and.s: On work and rest, Keller focuses on sabbath: why we need it, where we find it and how to practice it, noting that rest is often harder for people than work.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-comm.s: Keller shows the passage is about community: the promise of true human community, what makes it up and where the power to live it comes from.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-upsi.s: Jesus’ Sermon on the Plain introduces a new kingdom that contrasts with the present one in its patterns, power and outcomes, reversing worldly values and running against natural instinct.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/money-an.s: Keller contrasts the values of the world’s kingdom with the upside-down kingdom Jesus brings, closing with both an encouragement and a warning.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Asks whether there is good news for people who lack everything, looking at how Jesus’ poverty and teaching show God’s compassion for the desperate.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/how-chr.s: Luke 6:20–26: believers may face sorrow, poverty and rejection for a time yet remain deeply blessed because God’s reign is coming.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/blessed-.s: Keller argues that caring for and getting involved with the poor is a defining mark of the church, and that the gospel shapes believers to know, identify with and love the poor.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/hope-thy.s: Keller examines what it means to pray “Thy kingdom come,” explaining the kingdom of God, how one enters it and how it shapes prayer.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Depending on wealth for security in an uncertain future pulls people from genuine hope in God (Luke 6:24).

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/bec.s: Christians already belong to God as His children, so loving enemies and showing mercy doesn’t earn adoption but proves the family resemblance.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/jus.s: God lavishly rewards those who give, so believers can give freely, expecting their return from Him rather than from people.

https://coe22.com/sermons/when-he-asks/w.s: Luke 6:43–49: accepting God’s love through Jesus transforms how we live and the fruit we bear.

https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/h.s: We can keep praying without giving up, since God is nothing like the unjust judge; He gladly hears His chosen children.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/alw.s: The parable of the persistent widow: keep praying until Christ returns, since persevering prayer sustains faith and God eagerly vindicates His chosen ones.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/thi.s: Our standing before God rests not on moral or religious goodness but solely on Christ’s righteousness credited through faith.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/inside-o.s: The Pharisee and the tax collector show that the problem of righteousness is universal, and Keller contrasts a failed outside-in approach with a working inside-out one.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/generosi.s: Generosity reaches beyond money to the depths of the heart, so a person can give financially without being radically generous. Keller examines its source, signs and the means of growing in it.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/let.s: Christ’s followers should clear away whatever blocks children from coming to Him: pride, unbelieving parents, weak teaching, poor planning, limited space.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/tur.s: From the rich young ruler: only God can transform a heart so that losing wealth grieves less than gaining Jesus delights.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-grac.s: Using the rich young ruler, Keller argues the gospel should transform our relationship with money, which can be spiritually dangerous, and explains why and how to escape.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/generosi.s: Generosity is more than giving money, Keller says, using the rich young ruler to show the danger money poses, why it is so dangerous and how to escape it.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/som.s: Through the rich young ruler, clinging to idols creates hidden bondage, while trusting Jesus brings true freedom.

https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/d.s: Jesus uses headline tragedies to call onlookers to repentance; news is worthwhile only when it produces humility, compassion and action, not numbness.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/don.s: When tragedies make headlines, Jesus urges everyone to turn back to God, treating survival as a merciful chance to repent rather than a sign of innocence.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/unl.s: Tragedy doesn’t reveal greater guilt in its victims; everyone is equally sinful, so all must repent to escape eternal judgment.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/sufferi.s: Suffering tempts us to see ourselves as blameless victims, but Jesus urged everyone to turn from sin and return to God.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-para.s: Keller says repentance is the key to the Christian life and a sign of strength, not weakness, and explains why we need it, how to do it and how God produces it in us.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-fall.s: Keller looks at two tragedies Jesus mentions, Pilate’s massacre and a tower collapse that killed eighteen, and the question of why suffering seems unevenly distributed, and Jesus’ counterintuitive response.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jes.s: Jesus calls men and women to honor each other as fellow heirs of God’s promises, with humble, servant-hearted relationships judged by God’s Word.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: How a God who rules everything relates to Satan and his forces, drawing on Luke 13:11–16 to show divine authority over spiritual evil.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-para.s: Christianity is not merely ideals or a point of view to adopt, Keller argues, but a ruling power, one of new life and growth.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Luke wrote his Gospel and Acts to convince Theophilus that Christianity is true, using careful investigation and reliable eyewitness sources.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-bibl.s: Luke’s opening statements show the Bible is truth, Keller says: truth about a man, Jesus, and truth for the heart as well as the mind.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-true.s: Luke’s opening verses answer modern claims that the Gospels are unreliable legends, presenting them as true history, with the gospel centered on Jesus, grounded in truth and told as a story.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/how.s: Seeking evidence for faith is legitimate, but demanding more proof than a humble heart needs is wrong, as Zechariah’s doubt contrasts with Mary’s humble questions.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/adv.s: Advent and Christmas exist to stir up worship, since God’s arrival in the world moves hearts to adore and praise Him.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/p.s: As John the Baptist readied Israel, Advent readies our hearts through honest reflection on dependence on Christ, self-searching, joyful anticipation and Scripture.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jes.s: Through Luke 1–2, Luke writes so Theophilus can firmly know God, Jesus as the God-man, salvation through His blood, and faith like Mary’s.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/who.s: The differing genealogies (Jacob in Matthew, Heli in Luke) can be reconciled: one traces physical ancestry, the other legal succession to David’s throne.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Life beginning at conception is a wondrous, God-made gift bearing His image, and Luke 1 portrays the unborn child as a person.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Pursuing emotional highs leaves people hollow, while the Spirit quietly fills them by turning their attention to Christ (Luke 1:26–37).

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/marys-so.s: Christmas is God becoming human, which shows God is greater than we thought, we are more sinful than we thought and God is more loving than we think, followed by Mary’s three-stage response as a model.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-firs.s: Keller argues Mary, a teenage unwed mother, was the first person to receive the gospel in faith, and walks through the message she heard, her questioning and her surrender.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/what-ch.s: Luke 1:30–37: slows down to see how the angel’s announcement to Mary reveals who Jesus truly is.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Advent celebrates a Jewish king whose kingdom lasts forever, which Gentiles share by faith as heirs of Abraham’s promise.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/seven-r.s: Christmas worship is grounded in Jesus’ birth and death, which together free people to enjoy God forever.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-deit.s: Keller urges listeners not to go numb to the familiar Christmas story but to hear that God became flesh, a truth that should challenge both the mind and the heart.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/marys-so.s: Keller examines Mary’s song, which he calls the first Christmas carol, asking what prompts her to sing and what themes it emphasizes.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/med.s: Mary’s praise shows that God lifts up the humble and brings down the proud, and we glorify Him most by delighting in His mercy.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/a-c.s: Mary’s Magnificat reveals a surprising God who exalts the humble and rescues the weak, and who is most glorified when His people find deepest joy in Him.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/m.s: Mary and Elizabeth show that true praise comes from humble people who marvel that a great God stoops to notice them.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jes.s: Though John the Baptist was a remarkable forerunner, Jesus far surpasses him as the one who secures the salvation John pointed toward.
From Luke 1: Jesus is God’s mighty deliverer, conquering sin and Satan to free believers from fear and guilt so they can live righteously.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/t.s: Zechariah declares God’s promised redemption as already accomplished, since faith treats a divine promise as settled and Jesus fulfills God’s long-awaited visit.

https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/t.s: Christmas’s greatest blessing is freedom from sin and the devil, grasped only after recognizing our soul’s fatal sickness and the enemy’s threat.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-birt.s: Keller argues Christmas is God’s plan to deal with evil, suffering and death for good, exploring the fact and pattern of Christmas to show how God addresses the world’s darkness.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/f.s: God uses even mighty rulers and global events to advance His purposes for ordinary believers, so hardship never means He has stopped caring.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/god-sen.s: Jesus’ birth was a real historical event directed by God the Father, not a myth or a false prophet’s vision.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/n.s: God could have arranged lodging for Jesus at His birth but chose otherwise, since that would have strayed from the path to the cross.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/unto-us.s: Asks whether Christmas should center on holiday customs or on Christ and His saving sacrifice (Luke 2:8–14).

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/respondi.s: Keller asks how to respond to Jesus’ birth and answers with three things: hear well, make peace and fear not.

https://coe22.com/sermons/unwrapping-chr.s: Christmas from the manger: the angel’s “fear not” and good news of great joy for all the people.

https://www.desiringgod.org/solid-joys/p.s: Christmas peace belongs to those with faith, since trusting God’s promises unlocks His peace.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/christma.s: The peace Jesus came to bring is the heart of Christmas, Keller says, and he covers what that peace is not, what it is and how people receive and live it out.

https://www.desiringgod.org/labs/the-nig.s: The shepherds didn’t keep quiet that night; they shared the news of Jesus’ birth, and we’re asked to follow their example.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/sim.s: Jesus’ arrival opens a new stage in redemptive history that fulfills the Old Testament law and prophets rather than canceling them, so the most faithful saints welcomed Him.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/pre.s: God readies people to welcome Christ by awakening a longing for consolation and redemption that only Christ can provide, as in Simeon, Anna and Martin Luther.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/fas.s: Christians should fast with longing for Christ’s return, as Anna yearned for the Messiah; we who know Him should hunger for His coming even more.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: From Luke 2:36–38, an aged woman’s devoted fasting urges Christians to passionately long for Jesus’ return.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Luke’s account of young Jesus in the temple is credible, revealing His unique sonship, His mission placed above family ties, and a model for seeking Scripture’s wisdom.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-exce.s: Keller reads the twelve-year-old Jesus in the temple and Jesus’ baptism together to show how to encounter him, with three points on sonship: Jesus as a boy, as a man and his followers.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/jesus-at.s: The boy Jesus confused both the religious experts and his anxious parents yet was exactly where he belonged, and still confounds expectations while inviting believers to share in his Father’s feast.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/long-liv.s: The women at the empty tomb, gently rebuked by angels for seeking the living among the dead, made three errors we repeat when we live as if Jesus were still dead: denying the miracle, the meaning and the spiritual reality of the resurrection.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/he-.s: Jesus’ resurrection proves God’s victory over death, sin and evil, assuring believers of forgiveness, restoration, freedom and the triumph of God’s good plans.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/two-meet.s: Keller argues Luke chose the few resurrection appearances he records because they reveal the meaning of the resurrection most fully, and examines the disciples’ spiritual blindness and how to meet the risen Christ personally.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/set.s: Worship rekindles hearts when it first dislodges self from the center of our lives, then places Christ and the gospel’s accomplishment there instead.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: From Jesus eating fish after His resurrection (Luke 24): God affirms physical, embodied life and does not treat the body as a disposable shell.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/doubt-jo.s: The risen Jesus answers doubt with reasoned argument, meets emotional needs by eating with his disciples, redirects their lives by sending them out, and shows them his wounded hands and feet, so he can do the same for believers now.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-disc.s: Believers have a future resurrection to await and a present spiritual resurrection to experience now, Keller argues, and the future hope only shapes our lives when the present experience is real.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Examines how the boundaries of the Old Testament canon can be determined and which books belong within it.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/jesus-as.s: Faith is less a belief we choose than a reality that takes hold of us, Keller argues, and presents Jesus as a prophetic teacher who provides for people, pursues them and reveals the truth.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/tau.s: Acts shows believers what to believe about Jesus and how to read the Old Testament as Jesus taught, as seen in Peter’s and Paul’s sermons.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Jesus’ ascension should bring joy, not sorrow, because it assures a future reunion, restores Him to glory and secures lasting benefits for believers.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-call.s: Once Jesus is recognized as the Christ, following him means a new priority, a new identity and a new mercy, Keller argues.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/you.s: Our true identity emerges not through self-focus but by forgetting ourselves and being absorbed in God, who lets us become most fully who we were made to be.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/gai.s: Following Christ into mission means giving up comforts, dying to self-rule and treasuring Jesus most, because surrendering what we cannot keep secures what is eternal.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-glor.s: Keller uses the transfiguration to answer the recurring question “who is this?”, as a key to who Jesus is, what he came to do and how to connect with him.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/he-.s: Jesus knew His journey to Jerusalem meant suffering and death and chose it deliberately, so His followers embrace sacrificial service rather than worldly glory.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Jesus tests prospective disciples by spelling out the cost, probing whether He is what they value most above home, family and comfort.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/let-the-.s: Keller argues Jesus doesn’t make discipleship easy: he makes would-be followers stop and count the cost, entering his kingdom, recognizing its demands and understanding its greatness.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/money-an.s: Jesus sets a standard of sacrificial giving that seems unreasonable at first, then shows such generosity is actually reasonable, in Keller’s series on money and possessions in Luke.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/who.s: Jesus calls believers to host people unable to return the favor, since the guest list exposes whether comfort and payback or Christ is our true treasure.

https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/wha.s: Good things God gives, like work, family and comfort, can become excuses that keep us from delighting in Him more.

https://coe22.com/sermons/john/john-wk-0.s: John 4:46–5:18: asks whether you want to be healed, and argues that in Christ your past need not define your future.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-heal.s: Saving faith isn’t a personality trait or talent for some people, Keller argues: it begins with reason, grows into trust, rests on the reliability of Jesus rather than the strength of one’s faith, and eventually loves Christ for who he is.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/hea.s: Jesus healed only a few at Bethesda, and His main purpose was holiness, so meeting Him in our brokenness matters more than perfect physical health.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: From John 5:1–18: Jesus is far from aloof, moved by deep compassion for those who suffer.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-pool.s: Keller looks at the healing of the lame man at the pool of Bethesda, the third of John’s signs, through the pool, the man and the Sabbath controversy to show what it reveals about Jesus.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jes.s: Jesus healed a sick man at Bethesda to free him from sin, and because He acts in harmony with the Father, honoring the Son means honoring God.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: Jesus’ miracles in John 5 are signs directing us past physical cures toward a more profound spiritual restoration, holiness.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/you.s: Believers already possess eternal life, so although their bodies die they never truly die, since their communion with God is unbreakable.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: From John 5:25–29: Jesus’ spoken word will summon every person who has ever lived out of death, a truth presented as astonishing.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Jesus, who has life in himself, will raise all the dead by His voice, and judgment will reveal whether faith bore the fruit of good works.

https://www.desiringgod.org/light-and-tr.s: From John 5:25–29: Jesus is the source of life because, like the Father, He has life in Himself as God and gives it to others.
From John 5:30–47: why people crave others’ praise and how Christ can free them from that restless need.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jes.s: The Old Testament points to Christ throughout, so anyone claiming to know, honor or love God must acknowledge and receive Jesus as the Son.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/finding-.s: Jesus answers challenges to his claims by citing three witnesses: John the Baptist, his own works and the Scriptures. Keller draws out three things Jesus believed about the Bible: its authority, its unity and its living power.

https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the.s: Craving other people’s approval blocks people from trusting Jesus, and finding deeper satisfaction in Christ frees them from that craving.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/bible-en.s: Keller describes Jesus debating diligent Bible students who still fail to hear what God is saying, and explores how God speaks through Scripture, why people miss it and how to truly listen.

https://coe22.com/sermons/john/john-wk-1.s: John 11: because believers are new people in Christ, they no longer need to live by the habits of their old selves.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/out-from.s: Keller examines the raising of Lazarus, the seventh and climactic sign in John, drawing out who Jesus is through his time with Mary and Martha and what he came to do through his encounter with the dead Lazarus.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/truth-te.s: Keller shows how Jesus meets the grief of Lazarus’ death with truth for Martha, tears with Mary, anger at the tomb and grace for everyone.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-furi.s: Keller presents Jesus at Lazarus’ tomb as Immanuel, God actually present with people in their circumstances, and explores who Jesus is and why he came.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/the-humi.s: Part of a series on real character change, the sermon examines how Jesus defines humility, meekness, and how believers can grow in it through heart-level transformation by Christ.

https://coe22.com/sermons/john/john-wk-1.s: John 8:12–59: the gospel sets us free; we all serve something, and only Jesus brings freedom through surrender.

https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/sent-to-.s: Keller asks whether following Jesus limits or preserves human freedom, arguing the answer is complex, and explores the nature of freedom, what threatens it and Jesus as its true liberator.
